title: Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the four classic obstructive diseases: asthma, bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis, and emphysema. In each, air has trouble leaving the lung, so the FEV1 falls more than the FVC and air is trapped behind narrowed or collapsing airways. The diseases differ in where the lesion lies and what drives it: reversible Th2 inflammation in asthma, destroyed bronchial walls in bronchiectasis, mucus hypersecretion and small airway disease in chronic bronchitis, and loss of alveolar walls in emphysema. Board questions give a sputum finding, a histologic feature, a spirometry pattern, a DLCO, or a blood gas and ask you to name the disease and explain the mechanism, so this chapter teaches you to reason from the lesion to the test result.
prerequisites: Lung volumes, spirometry, and the flow-volume loop (PU-6)
Airway resistance, elastic recoil, and dynamic airway compression (PU-5)
Ventilation-perfusion matching, the alveolar gas equation, and DLCO (PU-7)
Type I hypersensitivity and Th2 cytokines (IM-15-C)
Interpretation of arterial blood gases and acid-base compensation

connections.how: Th2 cytokines, IgE, mast cells, eosinophils, and neutrophil elastase are the effector mechanisms behind asthma and emphysema.
Cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia are leading causes of bronchiectasis because both prevent mucus clearance.
Chronic suppurative bronchiectasis keeps serum amyloid A high and can cause systemic AA amyloidosis.
In alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, misfolded protein retained in hepatocytes injures the liver while the low serum level exposes the lung to elastase.
Chronic alveolar hypoxia in COPD constricts and remodels pulmonary arterioles, causing pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

terms.def: A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio caused by increased airway resistance or lost elastic recoil, usually with a normal or increased total lung capacity.
Exaggerated bronchoconstriction in response to stimuli that barely affect normal airways.
Structural change of chronically inflamed airways, including goblet cell hyperplasia, subepithelial fibrosis, gland enlargement, and smooth muscle hypertrophy.
Whorled mucus plugs containing shed epithelial cells, found in the sputum of asthmatic patients.
Slender bipyramidal crystals formed from the eosinophil protein galectin-10, marking eosinophilic inflammation.
An exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic blood pressure, greater than 10 mmHg.
The thickness of the submucosal gland layer divided by the thickness of the bronchial wall between the epithelium and the cartilage.
The gas-exchanging unit distal to a terminal bronchiole: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli.
A serine protease inhibitor made by hepatocytes that neutralizes neutrophil elastase in the lung.
The diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide, which reflects the alveolar capillary surface area and the capillary blood volume available for gas transfer.
The point along an airway during forced expiration where pressure inside the airway equals pleural pressure; airways downstream of it can be compressed.
Right ventricular hypertrophy, dilation, or failure caused by pulmonary hypertension that results from disease of the lungs or their vessels.

blocks.text: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation that produces airway hyperresponsiveness and recurrent episodes of obstruction that reverse, fully or largely, either spontaneously or with a bronchodilator. Three processes narrow the lumen together: smooth muscle contraction, mucosal edema, and mucus plugging. Because airway resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of the radius, a modest loss of caliber produces a large rise in resistance.

Atopic (allergic) asthma is the most common form. It usually begins in childhood, often with eczema or allergic rhinitis in the patient or family, and is a type I hypersensitivity. Dendritic cells carry inhaled allergen to lymph nodes and present it to naive CD4 T cells. Epithelial alarmins (thymic stromal lymphopoietin, IL-25, IL-33) and IL-4 steer these cells toward the Th2 lineage. IL-4 and IL-13 switch B cells to IgE, which binds high-affinity Fc epsilon receptors on mast cells; IL-5 drives eosinophil production, recruitment, and survival; and IL-13 stimulates goblet cell mucus production and hyperresponsiveness.

blocks.title: Atopic asthma: early and late phase
steps: Inhaled allergen cross-links IgE on sensitized mast cells
Mast cells release histamine, cysteinyl leukotrienes, and PGD2
Early phase within minutes: bronchospasm, edema, mucus
Mediators and Th2 cytokines recruit eosinophils
Late phase hours later: eosinophil proteins injure epithelium
Repeated injury and repair remodel the airway
blocks.caption: The early phase is mast cell mediator release; the late phase is leukocyte inflammation that sustains hyperresponsiveness.

blocks.text: Nonatopic asthma shows no evidence of allergen sensitization, and serum IgE is often normal. The airways are still hyperresponsive, and attacks are set off by stimuli that do not act through IgE. These triggers also provoke attacks in atopic patients.

blocks.title: Nonatopic triggers and their mechanisms
rows: Epithelial injury and inflammation increase hyperresponsiveness; the most common trigger of exacerbations
Heat and water loss make airway lining fluid hyperosmolar, so mast cells release mediators; bronchospasm typically peaks minutes after exercise ends
Blocking COX removes bronchoprotective PGE2 and diverts arachidonic acid to 5-lipoxygenase, overproducing cysteinyl leukotrienes; accompanied by chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps
Direct epithelial irritation and reflex bronchoconstriction; some occupational agents also cause sensitization
blocks.caption: Different triggers converge on the same hyperresponsive, inflamed airway.

blocks.text: Repeated attacks leave a recognizable pathology. In fatal status asthmaticus the lungs are overinflated and the bronchi are occluded by thick, tenacious mucus plugs. The cysteinyl leukotrienes (C4, D4, and E4), released in both atopic and aspirin-exacerbated disease, are potent bronchoconstrictors that also increase vascular permeability and mucus secretion. Remodeling explains why long-standing asthma can develop a partly fixed component of obstruction.

blocks.title: Sputum and histologic findings in asthma
cols: What it is and why it forms
rows: Whorled mucus plugs containing shed epithelial cells, from hypersecretion and epithelial sloughing
Crystals of galectin-10 released by eosinophils
Eosinophils in sputum and airway wall
IL-5 driven recruitment; eosinophil major basic protein damages epithelium
Goblet cell hyperplasia and submucosal gland enlargement
IL-13 driven mucus overproduction that forms plugs
Collagen laid down beneath the true basement membrane by activated myofibroblasts
More contractile mass, so each stimulus narrows the airway further
blocks.caption: Spirals and crystals are seen in sputum; the remaining features are seen in the airway wall.

sections.title: Acute asthma: physical findings, spirometry, and the blood gas

blocks.text: During an attack, resistance rises most in expiration, when falling lung volume and rising pleural pressure narrow the airways further. Expiration lengthens, air forced through narrowed bronchi makes their walls oscillate and produces wheezes, and air trapped behind closing airways hyperinflates the chest, giving a hyperresonant percussion note. Breathing at high lung volume flattens and shortens the diaphragm, so the sternocleidomastoid and scalene muscles are recruited and the patient becomes tachypneic and uses accessory muscles.

In a severe attack, forceful inspiration makes pleural pressure strongly negative. Venous return to the right ventricle increases and the septum bulges toward the left ventricle, blood pools in the expanded pulmonary vessels, and the negative pressure around the left ventricle raises its afterload. Left ventricular stroke volume and systolic pressure therefore fall with each inspiration, and a fall greater than 10 mmHg is pulsus paradoxus. Inability to speak in full sentences and a quiet chest, where so little air moves that wheezing fades, also signal severe obstruction.

Spirometry shows an obstructive pattern: FEV1/FVC, FEV1, and peak expiratory flow fall. The defining feature is reversibility, conventionally a rise in FEV1 of at least 12% and 200 mL after an inhaled bronchodilator given as a diagnostic test. Between attacks spirometry may be normal, and hyperresponsiveness can then be shown by bronchoprovocation with methacholine. DLCO is normal or slightly increased because the alveolar membrane is intact.

blocks.title: Evolution of the blood gas in acute asthma
steps: Bronchospasm creates low V/Q units; PaO2 falls
Hypoxemia and airway receptors drive hyperventilation
Well ventilated units unload CO2: respiratory alkalosis
Air trapping raises the work of breathing
Respiratory muscles fatigue; alveolar ventilation falls
PaCO2 returns to normal, then rises: respiratory acidosis
blocks.caption: A normal PaCO2 in a breathless, tachypneic asthmatic marks the turn toward respiratory failure.

blocks.text: Why does PaCO2 fall while PaO2 stays low? Hyperventilation of the better ventilated units removes extra CO2, because the CO2 content curve is nearly linear in the physiologic range. Those units cannot add extra O2, because their hemoglobin is already almost fully saturated, so they cannot offset the desaturated blood from low V/Q units. PaCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation, so once fatigue reduces ventilation, PaCO2 climbs back through the normal range of 35 to 45 mmHg.

blocks.title: Reading serial gases in an asthma attack
blocks.text: A 22-year-old woman arrives wheezing. First gas: pH 7.48, PaCO2 30 mmHg, PaO2 65 mmHg, an acute respiratory alkalosis with hypoxemia, which is expected because she is hyperventilating. Three hours later she is still wheezing, with a respiratory rate of 32, accessory muscle use, and fainter breath sounds. Second gas: pH 7.40, PaCO2 40 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg. The numbers look normal, but her drive to breathe is maximal, so a PaCO2 of 40 means alveolar ventilation is no longer keeping pace. Together with the worsening hypoxemia and quieter chest, this indicates muscle fatigue and impending respiratory failure, and the next gas would show a rising PaCO2 with acidemia.

Bronchiectasis is permanent dilation of bronchi and bronchioles caused by destruction of the smooth muscle and elastic tissue in their walls. Two ingredients are required: obstruction or impaired clearance of secretions, and chronic necrotizing infection. Either can come first, and each sustains the other, which is why the disease progresses once established.

blocks.title: The vicious cycle of bronchiectasis
steps: Obstruction or impaired clearance retains secretions
Bacteria colonize the pooled mucus
Neutrophils release elastase and other proteases
Muscle and elastic tissue of the wall are destroyed
Weakened bronchi dilate permanently
Dilated bronchi pool even more secretions
blocks.caption: Infection and poor clearance feed each other, so dilation becomes irreversible.

blocks.title: Major causes of bronchiectasis
rows: Autosomal recessive CFTR defect dehydrates airway surface liquid; thick mucus is colonized by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus

Autosomal recessive axoneme defects, most often of the dynein arms, immobilize respiratory cilia, sperm flagella, and the embryonic nodal cilia that set left-right asymmetry; with situs inversus it is Kartagener syndrome
Diffuse, often middle and lower lobes; chronic sinusitis and otitis
IgE and IgG mediated reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus colonizing the airways of patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis; eosinophilia, very high IgE, mucus plugs
Localized obstruction traps secretions and infection beyond it
Severe necrotizing infection and immune deficiency
Necrotizing pneumonia (for example pertussis, measles, tuberculosis) or hypogammaglobulinemia allows repeated infection
Follows the infection; post-tuberculous disease favors the upper lobes
blocks.caption: Every cause either blocks an airway, defeats mucociliary clearance, or weakens host defense.

blocks.text: Grossly, the lower lobes are usually affected bilaterally, most severely in the more vertical airways. The bronchi may dilate to several times normal size and can be traced almost to the pleura. Histology shows intense acute and chronic inflammation with ulceration and desquamation of the mucosa, sometimes squamous metaplasia, and peribronchial fibrosis in long-standing disease. On CT the dilated bronchus is wider than its companion artery (signet ring sign) and its walls fail to taper (tram tracks).

The manifestations follow from pooled, infected secretions. Patients have a daily cough with copious, often foul-smelling purulent sputum, worse with changes in position. Hemoptysis occurs because chronic inflammation enlarges the bronchial arteries, which carry systemic pressure, and erosion of these vessels can bleed heavily. Digital clubbing accompanies chronic suppuration, although its mechanism is not fully established. Persistent inflammation keeps IL-6 driven hepatic production of serum amyloid A high, and its fragments deposit as AA amyloid, often first appearing as proteinuria. Other complications include lung abscess, metastatic brain abscess, and, with extensive disease, pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. Spirometry usually shows obstruction.

blocks.predict: A 30-year-old man has chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, dextrocardia, and infertility with immotile sperm. Which structure is defective, and why are the heart and the sperm affected?
blocks.explain: The dynein arms of the microtubule axoneme. Without them, respiratory cilia cannot clear mucus, and sperm flagella cannot beat. Motile cilia at the embryonic node normally create a leftward flow that sets left-right asymmetry, so without it organ position is left to chance and about half of patients have situs inversus. Infertility in cystic fibrosis has a different cause: congenital absence of the vas deferens.

sections.title: Chronic bronchitis and the blue bloater

blocks.text: Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically: a productive cough on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, after other causes are excluded. Cigarette smoking is the dominant cause, with air pollution and occupational dusts contributing. Most smokers with COPD have both chronic bronchitis and emphysema in varying proportions.

In the large cartilaginous bronchi, irritants cause hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the submucosal mucous glands and an increase in goblet cells. The Reid index quantifies gland enlargement: the thickness of the gland layer divided by the thickness of the wall from the epithelium to the cartilage. It is normally below about 0.4 and exceeds 0.5 in chronic bronchitis. Smoke also impairs ciliary beating and causes squamous metaplasia, so mucus is overproduced and poorly cleared, which produces the chronic cough. Infection does not start the disease but maintains it and causes acute exacerbations.

Hypersecretion in large airways does not by itself limit airflow. Obstruction comes from small airway disease (chronic bronchiolitis) in airways less than 2 mm in diameter: goblet cell metaplasia, mucus plugging, inflammation, and peribronchiolar fibrosis narrow the lumen.

Narrowed and plugged small airways leave many alveoli poorly ventilated but still perfused. Blood leaving these low V/Q units is poorly oxygenated, so hypoxemia appears early. As obstruction and the work of breathing increase, and in patients whose ventilatory drive is blunted, alveolar ventilation falls and PaCO2 rises, producing a chronic respiratory acidosis that the kidneys compensate by retaining bicarbonate. Cyanosis appears when deoxygenated hemoglobin in capillary blood exceeds about 5 g/dL, and hypoxemia stimulates renal erythropoietin, so secondary polycythemia deepens the blue color and raises blood viscosity. Right heart failure produces the edema behind the name blue bloater.

blocks.title: From low V/Q units to cor pulmonale
steps: Plugged small airways lower alveolar PO2
Hypoxic vasoconstriction of pulmonary arterioles
Medial hypertrophy and fixed pulmonary hypertension
Right ventricular pressure overload and hypertrophy
Right ventricular failure: cor pulmonale
Raised jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema
blocks.caption: Acidosis strengthens hypoxic vasoconstriction, and polycythemia adds viscosity, so both worsen the pressure load.

blocks.predict: If alveolar PO2 in a patient with chronic bronchitis rose toward normal, what would happen to pulmonary arterial pressure early in the disease compared with after many years?
blocks.explain: Early, pressure would fall substantially because hypoxic vasoconstriction is a reversible smooth muscle response. After years of hypoxia, medial hypertrophy and remodeling of the arterioles are structural, so pressure falls only partly.

sections.title: Emphysema: patterns, alpha-1 antitrypsin, and hyperinflation

blocks.text: Emphysema is permanent enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with destruction of their walls and without obvious fibrosis. It results mainly from an imbalance between proteases and antiproteases, compounded by oxidant injury. When elastin is destroyed faster than it is repaired, alveolar walls and the capillaries within them are lost.

blocks.title: Protease and antiprotease imbalance in smokers
steps: Smoke activates alveolar macrophages and recruits neutrophils
Neutrophil elastase and macrophage metalloproteinases digest elastin
Oxidants inactivate alpha-1 antitrypsin
Alveolar walls and their capillaries are destroyed
Elastic recoil and airway tethering are lost
Small airways collapse in expiration: air trapping
blocks.caption: Smoking adds protease and removes antiprotease at the same time.

blocks.text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a serine protease inhibitor made by hepatocytes, encoded by SERPINA1 on chromosome 14, and its alleles are expressed codominantly. The normal allele is PiM. In the PiZZ genotype serum levels are about 10 to 15% of normal, leaving the entire acinus exposed to elastase. The Z protein also misfolds and polymerizes in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum, forming PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules that can cause neonatal hepatitis and cirrhosis.

blocks.title: Patterns of emphysema
rows: Respiratory bronchioles in the center; distal alveoli spared
Cigarette smoking; the most common pattern
Entire acinus, from respiratory bronchiole to alveoli
Distal acinus next to pleura and septa
Subpleural, upper lobes, often near scars
Bullae that rupture: spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults
blocks.caption: Smoke injures the center of the acinus first; deficiency of the inhibitor leaves the whole acinus unprotected.

blocks.text: Loss of elastic recoil is the central physiologic defect. Recoil normally drives passive expiration, and the alveolar walls attached around small airways hold them open by radial traction. With both lost, the equal pressure point moves toward the alveoli during expiration, small airways collapse, and air is trapped. The lungs hyperinflate: the anteroposterior chest diameter increases (barrel chest), the diaphragms flatten, percussion is hyperresonant, and breath sounds are distant. Pursed-lip breathing raises pressure inside the airways during expiration, which moves the equal pressure point toward the mouth into cartilage-supported airways and slows exhalation, so less collapse occurs. Patients increase their ventilation to keep blood gases near normal, at a high work of breathing, so they are dyspneic, thin, and pink, the classic pink puffer.

blocks.predict: A 38-year-old nonsmoker has progressive dyspnea, hyperlucency at both lung bases, and elevated liver enzymes. Predict the emphysema pattern and explain why the liver is involved.
blocks.explain: Panacinar emphysema from alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ). Too little inhibitor reaches the lung, so elastase destroys the whole acinus, most in the lower lobes. The liver is injured not by a lack of protein but by misfolded Z protein that polymerizes and accumulates in hepatocytes.

sections.title: Testing in COPD: spirometry, lung volumes, DLCO, and blood gases

blocks.text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is persistent airflow limitation, usually from a mixture of small airway disease and emphysema. Spirometry establishes it: a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70. FEV1 falls more than FVC because narrowed or collapsing airways limit flow throughout forced expiration, and, unlike asthma, the obstruction does not reverse substantially after a bronchodilator. The expiratory limb of the flow-volume loop is scooped (concave). Severity is graded by FEV1 as a percentage of predicted (GOLD 1 to 4: at least 80%, 50 to 79%, 30 to 49%, below 30%).

Air trapping raises residual volume, functional residual capacity, and the RV/TLC ratio. Total lung capacity rises mainly from the emphysema component, because lost elastic recoil increases compliance and lets the lung expand further for the same inspiratory effort; with predominant chronic bronchitis TLC is normal or only mildly increased. A reduced TLC defines restriction, so a normal or increased TLC alongside a low FEV1/FVC excludes a restrictive process.

DLCO depends on alveolar capillary surface area and capillary blood volume. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls together with their capillaries, so DLCO falls. In chronic bronchitis the membrane is intact, so DLCO is normal; in asthma it is normal or increased.

The blood gases follow V/Q logic. In emphysema ventilation and perfusion are lost together, so matching is relatively preserved, and increased respiratory drive keeps PaO2 near normal and PaCO2 normal or low until late disease, although desaturation with exercise appears earlier because of the reduced diffusing surface. In chronic bronchitis, perfused alveoli behind plugged airways form low V/Q units from the start, giving early hypoxemia and hypercapnia, polycythemia, and cor pulmonale. Most patients have features of both.

blocks.title: Testing in emphysema, chronic bronchitis, and asthma
blocks.caption: DLCO and the blood gas separate the two COPD phenotypes; reversibility separates asthma.

blocks.title: Interpreting pulmonary function tests in a smoker
blocks.text: A 64-year-old former smoker has FEV1/FVC 0.55 after bronchodilator, FEV1 45% of predicted, TLC 125%, RV 180%, DLCO 40%, PaO2 76 mmHg, and PaCO2 38 mmHg. Step 1: a ratio below 0.70 that persists after bronchodilator means fixed obstruction, so this is COPD rather than asthma. Step 2: FEV1 of 45% places it in GOLD grade 3. Step 3: high TLC and RV show hyperinflation and air trapping, excluding restriction. Step 4: the low DLCO localizes the lesion to lost alveolar capillary surface. Step 5: near normal gases fit matched loss of ventilation and perfusion. The pattern is emphysema-predominant COPD. If instead DLCO were normal and PaCO2 52 mmHg with a high bicarbonate, the pattern would point to predominant chronic bronchitis.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology explain where each disease acts and how it is measured. The airway tree narrows from cartilaginous bronchi to bronchioles less than 2 mm across that depend on surrounding alveolar walls to stay open, so disease of the large airways (gland hyperplasia, bronchiectasis) causes cough and sputum, while disease of the small airways and acini (bronchiolitis, emphysema) causes most of the airflow limitation. Spirometry, lung volumes, DLCO, and the blood gas each test a different part of this system, and reading them together, rather than any one alone, distinguishes the diseases.

Immunology, biochemistry, and pathology supply the mechanisms. Asthma is Th2 and IgE driven inflammation; bronchiectasis and emphysema are protease injury from neutrophils, with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency linking a hepatocyte protein-folding defect to lung destruction; and chronic suppuration links to systemic AA amyloidosis. The clinical phenotypes are teaching models: most smokers have both emphysema and chronic bronchitis, some asthmatics develop fixed obstruction through remodeling, and bronchiectasis can coexist with COPD, so the test pattern describes the dominant process rather than a pure disease.

summary: Asthma is Th2 inflammation: IL-4 and IL-13 drive IgE, IL-5 drives eosinophils, and IL-13 drives mucus; mast cells cause the early phase and eosinophils the late phase.
Nonatopic triggers (viral infection, exercise and cold air, aspirin, irritants) act on hyperresponsive airways without IgE; aspirin shifts arachidonic acid to leukotrienes.
Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals appear in asthmatic sputum; remodeling adds goblet cells, a thick subepithelial basement membrane, and smooth muscle hypertrophy.
Acute asthma causes wheeze, prolonged expiration, hyperinflation, pulsus paradoxus above 10 mmHg when severe, and obstruction that reverses with a bronchodilator.
Early asthma gases show hypoxemia with low PaCO2; a normal or rising PaCO2 in a tachypneic patient means fatigue and impending respiratory failure.
Bronchiectasis is permanent dilation from poor clearance or obstruction plus necrotizing infection, causing copious purulent sputum, hemoptysis, clubbing, and AA amyloidosis.
Chronic bronchitis is productive cough for 3 months in 2 consecutive years with a Reid index above 0.5; low V/Q units cause early hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and cor pulmonale.
Centriacinar emphysema is upper lobe and smoking related, panacinar is lower lobe and alpha-1 antitrypsin related, and paraseptal causes bullae and spontaneous pneumothorax.
Lost elastic recoil and airway tethering cause expiratory airway collapse, air trapping, barrel chest, and pursed-lip breathing.
COPD shows post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 with increased RV and TLC; DLCO is low in emphysema and normal in chronic bronchitis.

verify: Bronchodilator reversibility is given as a rise in FEV1 of at least 12% and 200 mL; the 2022 ATS/ERS interpretation standard uses a change above 10% of the predicted value. Confirm which NABNE expects.
COPD is defined here by a fixed post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 (GOLD); some guidelines prefer the lower limit of normal. GOLD grade cutoffs are included as diagnostic classification only.
The normal Reid index is quoted variously as below about 0.4 or as 0.26 to 0.4; the threshold above 0.5 for chronic bronchitis is consistent across review sources.
Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin in PiZZ is quoted from about 10% to 20% of normal; this chapter uses about 10 to 15%.
The proportion of primary ciliary dyskinesia with situs inversus is given as about 50%; confirm if NABNE tests the figure.
Late-phase asthmatic reaction timing is quoted from about 2 to 8 hours after exposure in different texts, so the chapter says hours later without a fixed value.
The deoxygenated hemoglobin threshold for visible cyanosis is quoted as about 4 to 5 g/dL; this chapter uses about 5 g/dL.
Blue bloater and pink puffer are teaching stereotypes; confirm whether NABNE Part I still uses these terms and the eponym Kartagener syndrome.
The mechanism of digital clubbing in chronic suppurative lung disease is not settled (platelet-derived growth factors are the leading hypothesis), so it is not stated as fact.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: flow-volume-loops (normal, obstructive, and restrictive loops) and emphysema-acinus (centriacinar, panacinar, and paraseptal patterns within one acinus).
